## Barn 3 grow-out specification

I would set Barn 3 at **14,400 day-old Pekin ducklings per flock**.

| Measure | Barn 3 target |
|---|---:|
| Usable floor | 2,800 m² |
| Ducklings placed | **14,400** |
| Placement density | **5.14 ducklings/m²** |
| Assumed mortality/culls | 4.0% |
| Ducks marketed | **13,824** |
| Finish weight | 3.2 kg |
| Liveweight marketed | **44,237 kg** |
| Final bird density | 4.94 ducks/m² |
| Final liveweight density | **15.8 kg/m²** |

This is deliberately below the upper end reported for commercial Pekins. Published literature describes roughly 15–25 kg/m² as the usual target range, while Cornell’s floor-space allowance at six weeks equates to approximately 4.7 ducks/m². A solid-litter UK reference permits up to seven ducks/m², but that is more aggressive than I would use in a rebuilt, unproven barn. [Pekin welfare review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8777151/), [Cornell housing guidance](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/animal-health-diagnostic-center/programs/duck-research-laboratory/duck-housing-and-management), [UK duck guidance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/poultry-on-farm-welfare/ducks-mallard-and-pekin-welfare-recommendations)

For the first flock after the rebuild, I would actually place **13,800–14,000** unless the water system, drainage, minimum ventilation and alarms have already been load-tested. Move to 14,400 after Barn 3 demonstrates dry litter, acceptable ammonia and adequate peak water flow during weeks 5–6.

Because you sell spot, treat 14,400 as biological capacity, not an automatic placement. The sales-limited placement formula is:

\[
\text{ducklings placed}=
\frac{\text{live kg the market can clear}}{3.2 \times 0.96}
\]

For example, a reliable outlet for only 40,000 live kg supports about **13,000 placed**, not 14,400.

## Feed program and demand

Use a complete, pelleted waterfowl ration formulated for Pekins. A workable two-phase program is:

- Days 0–14: duck starter, approximately 20–22% crude protein.
- Days 15–42: grower/finisher, approximately 16.5–18% crude protein.
- Specify at least **55–60 mg niacin/kg feed** and have the mill formulate amino acids and minerals to the genetics being placed. Current husbandry literature suggests 60–80 mg/kg as a practical commercial specification. [Merck Pekin nutrient table](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/multimedia/table/nutrient-requirements-of-pekin-ducks), [Pekin husbandry review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8261006/)

Budget **7.0 kg of feed delivered per duckling placed**, including normal mortality and approximately 2–3% feed loss. That gives:

- Feed ordered: **100.8 metric tonnes**, or about **111 short tons**
- Delivered-feed conversion: **2.28 kg feed/kg liveweight marketed**
- Expected consumed-feed FCR: roughly **2.15–2.22**

| Age | Feed per placed bird | Barn total | Average delivery/day |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Days 1–7 | 0.25 kg | 3.60 t | 0.51 t |
| Days 8–14 | 0.75 kg | 10.80 t | 1.54 t |
| Days 15–21 | 1.10 kg | 15.84 t | 2.26 t |
| Days 22–28 | 1.30 kg | 18.72 t | 2.67 t |
| Days 29–35 | 1.65 kg | 23.76 t | 3.39 t |
| Days 36–42 | 1.95 kg | 28.08 t | **4.01 t** |
| **Total** | **7.00 kg** | **100.80 t** | — |

Published data vary materially by genetics and housing: one Pekin population consumed about 5.77 kg during days 15–42 alone, while Cornell-derived field data show about 6.4 kg cumulatively through six weeks at a lighter final weight. The 7.0 kg procurement budget is therefore reasonable for a 3.2 kg spot-market duck without leaving the barn short. [Feed-efficiency study](https://doi.org/10.5713/ajas.15.0577), [Cornell/Metzer consumption table](https://www.metzerfarms.com/daily-feed-water-ducklings.html)

Keep at least **three days of late-flock consumption** available: approximately 12 tonnes usable storage. Two bins are preferable so the starter/grower transition does not require running a bin completely empty.

## Water demand

Plan on approximately **4.2 litres of metered water per kilogram of feed**, or **425 m³ per flock** under normal conditions. Ducks may use appreciably more with open cups, excessive pressure, leakage or hot weather.

| Age | Normal water demand | Barn total |
|---|---:|---:|
| Week 1 | 1.55 L/placed bird | 22 m³ |
| Week 2 | 4.20 L | 60 m³ |
| Week 3 | 4.62 L | 67 m³ |
| Week 4 | 4.77 L | 69 m³ |
| Week 5 | 5.94 L | 86 m³ |
| Week 6 | 8.40 L | **121 m³** |
| **Total** | **29.5 L** | **425 m³** |

Week-six average is about **17.3 m³/day**. Design Barn 3 for:

- At least **25 m³/day** available in hot weather.
- Approximately **20–25 gallons/minute** instantaneous barn capacity, including line flushing.
- Water metering recorded daily.
- Water points over drained slats or dedicated drainage rather than directly over litter.
- Water access that permits bill immersion; Cornell suggests about 15 nipples per 100 growing ducks where nipples are used. [Cornell housing guidance](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/animal-health-diagnostic-center/programs/duck-research-laboratory/duck-housing-and-management)

A day-over-day water change above roughly 10–15%, after adjusting for temperature and bird age, should trigger a leak, pressure, health and feed-delivery check.

## Labor budget

For an automated feed and water barn, budget **450–550 labor hours per flock**, with **500 hours** as the planning figure.

|---|---:|
| Preheat, litter, sanitation and commissioning checks | 75 |
| Placement | 25 |
| Twice-daily flock walks, mortality and records | 145 |
| Water-area and litter management | 90 |
| Weighing, feed deliveries and routine maintenance | 45 |
| Catching/loading supervision and farm labor | 55 |
| Cleanout, wash and turnaround | 65 |
| **Total** | **500 hours** |

That equals about **0.035 hour per duckling placed**, or 7.9 labor hours per calendar day when pre- and post-flock work is spread over a 63-day flock/turnaround cycle. Contract catching, litter removal or shared work with the other barn should be removed from Barn 3’s internal-hours figure, but still retained as a cash cost.

Therefore, use:

- **Cash operating cost:** about **$2.50/kg liveweight**
- **Full cost:** about **$2.70/kg liveweight**
- Reasonable planning range: **$2.35–$3.05/kg**, depending mainly on duckling and delivered pellet prices.

This excludes outbound live haul if you pay it, financing interest, unusual veterinary events, manure value or disposal cost, and any processing or buyer deductions.

Useful sensitivities:

- Every **$50/short ton** change in feed price changes cost by about **$0.13/kg live**.

- Moving mortality from 4% to 6%, without a corresponding reduction in early feed and chick cost, adds roughly **$0.05–$0.07/kg**.

Indiana’s published standards are outcome-oriented—adequate water, shelter and protection from injury or disease—rather than a substitute for barn-specific capacity management. The stocking decision should ultimately be reduced if litter, ammonia, foot condition, panting, water access or market clearance deteriorates. [Indiana BOAH standards](https://www.in.gov/boah/animal-care-and-welfare/livestock-and-poultry-care-law/)

## Barn 3 grow-out specification

I would place **16,800 day-old Pekin ducklings**.

| Placement density | **6.0 ducklings/m²** |

That is a moderate commercial loading. A controlled study of modern commercial Pekin strains also used 6 birds/m², although its birds reached 3.6 kg at 42 days and averaged a 2.03 FCR under research-station conditions. [Lohmann commercial-strain trial](https://lohmann-breeders.com/lohmanninfo/performance-of-current-peking-duck-breeds/)

Indiana’s care standard is health-based—adequate water, shelter, treatment and an environment expected to maintain health—rather than a published numerical duck-density limit. - At least 2–3 flocks showing acceptable litter, gait, mortality and weight uniformity.
- Feeders, drinkers, ventilation, heat and emergency power all being sized for 16,800.
- Reducing to about **15,400–16,000** if Barn 3 has solid litter throughout, marginal summer ventilation or wet areas around drinkers.
- Not increasing above 16,800 merely because floor space appears available.

Plan another **10–15% water** for flushing, cleaning and ordinary loss:

- Bird/drinker demand: approximately **484 m³**

## Indiana permitting flag

IDEM counts animals at the **farm level**, not just Barn 3. Indiana’s CFO threshold is 30,000 poultry confined for at least 45 days in a year. Duck CAFO thresholds are 30,000 with solid manure handling but only 5,000 with a liquid system. Because you operate two barns—and Barn 3 was rebuilt—confirm the permitted farm capacity and IDEM’s classification of the manure system before placement. ## Barn 3 grow-out specification

I would place **18,000 day-old Pekin ducklings**.

That assumes:

- Usable floor: 2,800 m²
- Placement density: **6.43 ducklings/m²**
- Mortality/culls through day 42: **3.0%**

- Finish weight: 3.2 kg
- Liveweight shipped: approximately **55,870 kg**
- Expected final stocking: **19.96 kg liveweight/m²**
- Zero-mortality density: 20.57 kg/m²

I would treat **20 kg/m² as the planning density** and **22 kg/m² as a hard management trigger**, rather than deliberately stocking to 25 kg/m². Published commercial targets generally fall between 15 and 25 kg/m²; density should be expressed in final liveweight rather than birds/m². [Systematic review of Pekin welfare research](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8777151/)

This is an operating specification, not an Indiana statutory density limit. Barn 3 still falls under Indiana’s general livestock and poultry standards of care. [Indiana BOAH care law](https://www.in.gov/boah/animal-care-and-welfare/livestock-and-poultry-care-law/)

\text{Ducklings placed} =
\frac{2,800\ m² \times 20\ kg/m²}
{3.2\ kg \times 0.97}
=18,041
\]

Use waterfowl-formulated, non-medicated feed:

- Days 15–28: grower pellet, approximately 17–18%
- Days 29–42: finisher pellet, approximately 16–17%
- Require the mill to formulate specifically for Pekin ducks, including adequate niacin and amino acids.
- Do not use medicated poultry feed unless the medication is expressly labeled for ducks.

University of Kentucky guidance notes that properly balanced feed above 16% protein offers no demonstrated benefit after two weeks. [UK Extension duck feeding guidance](https://poultry.extension.org/articles/feeds-and-feeding-of-poultry/feeding-ducks-intended-for-consumption/)

Operational requirements:

- Normal late-flock water use: roughly **11 m³/day**
- Hot-weather design capacity: at least **15 m³/day**
- Recommended drinker availability: no more than about **10 ducks per functioning nipple**, requiring roughly **1,800 nipple positions**
- Provide supplemental easy-access starter drinkers for the first three days.

Published guidance permits up to 15 ducks per nipple, but the tighter 10:1 design allowance provides capacity for failed nipples, heat and uneven bird distribution. [2025 poultry-production guideline](https://www.q-s.de/services/files/downloadcenter/e-landwirtschaft/2025/leitfaeden/englisch/Guideline_Agriculture_Poultry_Production_01_01.2025.pdf) Nipple systems also carry substantially less bacterial contamination than open round drinkers.
